idiom_name: rayon par_iter/join over a global or ThreadPoolBuilder pool
implementation_notes: Rayon is the idiomatic Rust pool: a global work-stealing pool sized to the available parallelism backs par_iter, par_sort and join, and ThreadPoolBuilder::new().num_threads(n).build() creates a private pool when the global one must not be shared. Closures are the tasks, so threads, queues and joins disappear from the code; work stealing requires the work to be splittable, which is why rayon fits data-parallel batches best. Run synchronous third-party code inside pool.install() to keep it on pool threads, and keep per-task state in the closure because reused workers carry nothing between tasks except their stack.
pitfalls: A task that blocks (mutex, I/O, sleep) occupies a stealing worker and stalls unrelated work: rayon is for CPU-bound work.
Panics propagate to the join/collect caller and can poison shared state - treat a panic as a task failure and isolate it.
Nested pools re-enter scheduling and can deadlock when bounded; prefer rayon::join or install on the existing pool.

variants.name: Tokio blocking pool (spawn_blocking)
variants.idiom_name: tokio::task::spawn_blocking on the runtime's blocking pool
variants.implementation_notes: In an async service the pool you actually want is the runtime's: Tokio's multi-threaded scheduler multiplexes async tasks cooperatively and keeps a separate pool for spawn_blocking (and block_in_place on the multi-thread flavour), so synchronous libraries and CPU-heavy work do not stall the reactor. It replaces a hand-written pool entirely for that use case - size the runtime with worker_threads, bound concurrency with semaphores or a dedicated runtime, and rely on JoinHandle for completion.
pitfalls: spawn_blocking tasks cannot be aborted once running (documented): a runaway blocking task holds its thread.
The blocking pool is bounded and shared; long tasks delay every other spawn_blocking in the process.
Blocking directly inside an async task stalls a worker for every task multiplexed on it.

variants.name: std::thread + channel (no dependencies)
variants.idiom_name: std::thread workers over std::sync::mpsc with join-based shutdown
variants.implementation_notes: Without crates the pool is std::thread::spawn workers each owning a Receiver (or sharing one behind Arc<Mutex<Receiver>>/crossbeam-channel) and looping over messages, with channel disconnect or an Arc<AtomicBool> as the stop signal and JoinHandle::join at shutdown; std::thread::scope bounds thread lifetimes so borrowed data needs no Arc. This is the dependency-free fallback and the place to build an exact queue policy; tasks must be Send + 'static unless the pool is scoped.
pitfalls: An mpsc Receiver cannot be shared without a Mutex (only one receiver exists): use crossbeam-channel or Arc<Mutex<Receiver>>.
Dropping a JoinHandle detaches the thread silently: exit paths must join, and a panic poisons the queue Mutex so the worker loop turns into a panic storm.
A worker panic only surfaces at join - track task failures instead of assuming the pool survived.
